title: Sundial Freight — SLO fuzz testing and cost sensitivity exploration
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

This note captures the results and open items from the Sundial Freight POC stress and SLO‑fuzzing sessions (week of 2029-01-08). Goal was not to present a definitive capacity plan, but to map failure surfaces and quantify cost tradeoffs for a conversational logistics assistant operating at mixed query sizes and high microburst risk (rush-hour dispatch and API façade spikes).

Top-level findings (TL;DR):
- With KV prefix caching enabled and a conservative batching policy (max_batch=16, latency target 180ms), p95 generation latency under steady load (QPS=60) stays under 220ms for the 7B model variant.
- Short microbursts (30s–90s) at 8x baseline QPS drove queueing-induced p99 spikes to >2.1s when cold KV caches and no warmup policy were present.
- Enabling model-tier fallback (7B -> 3B quantized) reduced p99 during overload by ~45% but increased token cost by ~4% due to more retries and fallbacks executed; however perceived user latency improved in 72% of simulated conversational sessions.
- Quantization to 4-bit (int4) reduced per-token GPU cost ~35% but increased median latency by 12ms due to CAST penalties in our runtime on the tested GPU (A100-sim). Tradeoff acceptable for background rerank/embedding workloads, less so for low-latency chat turns.
- Warmup strategies (proactive KV prefetch + coldstart p95 limiters) recovered tail latency quickly — we observed a 60% reduction in 2-minute post-burst tail compared to no-warmup baseline.

Test matrix and environment:
- Customer workload sketch: short chat turns (avg prompt tokens=40, avg gen tokens=80), intermittent long-form generation (avg prompt tokens=600) triggered by 'summarize-route' flows at ~5% of requests. Peak burst factor observed in traffic trace: 7.6x baseline for 45–120s.
- Models used: open-7b-v2 (float16), open-3b-int4 (quantized), and a control open-7b-int8 profile.
- Infra: single-region cluster (us-west2) running dedicated G4/GPU equivalent nodes; runtime stack: Redwood serving-runtime commit rwd-serve@2029-01-04 + local kernel selection shim.
- Experiment harness: locust + synthetic trace generator (session-aware), with replayed inter-arrival times from Sundial production logs (anon).
- Measured metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 generation latency, end-to-end latency (api ingress -> last token), throughput (requests/sec), GPU utilization, and estimated cost per 1M tokens (based on committed instance price).

Detailed experiments and observations:
1) Steady-state throughput sweep (30–120 QPS)
- Setup: warm cache (KV warmed with 100k popular prefixes), mixed requests (90% chat short, 10% long form).
- Results: 7B-fp16 at 60 QPS: p95=210ms, p99=420ms, GPU util=68%. At 100 QPS p95 approached 330ms and GPU util ~92% with occasional scheduler backpressure.
- Notes: continuous-batching gains plateau after 64 concurrent in-flight requests; beyond that latency climbs sharply. We think changing kernel selection for medium sequence lengths can yield 8–12% improvement.

2) Microburst injection (burst factor 1.5x -> 8x, durations 15s, 45s, 120s)
- Cold-cache condition: no KV warmup, nodes scaled to meet baseline.
- Short bursts (15–30s) at 4–8x: queue length increases rapidly; p99 jumps above 1.6–2.2s depending on burst magnitude. Queue saturation observed on the scheduler layer, not at GPU driver layer.
- Longer bursts (90–120s): autoscaler started new pods at ~75s but new pods took 110–140s to become available (image pull + model load). This means autoscaling alone cannot protect against short bursts; pre-warmed standby or burst credits recommended.

3) Fallback policy experiment (7B -> 3B-int4 fallback with strict route-level SLO)
- Behavior: requests first attempted on primary model; if queueing > threshold (inflight>64) we routed new requests to fallback per policy.
- Result: 35–50% reduction in p99 under heavy burst conditions; overall token cost delta +3.7% because the fallback produced slightly longer outputs (model verbosity difference) and we compensated with client retry rules in the harness.
- Customer note: fallback must be transparent to user (response header + telemetry) so downstream product metrics can detect quality regressions.

4) Quantization and kernel tradeoffs
- int4 model reduced GPU memory footprint enough to consolidate extra replica in node; cost-per-token reduced by ~35%. However, on our tested kernel stack median generation latency increased by ~12ms for short-turn workloads. For reranking/embeds, the throughput gains outweigh latency penalty.
- Action: recommend int4 for batch/async workloads, int8 or fp16 for latency-critical chat. Consider a per-route quantization policy.

5) Cache warmup strategies and observed gains
- Passive warmup (prefetch top-10k prefixes at boot) reduced cold-start p95 by ~48% in our long-form flows.
- Active warmup (anticipatory based on traffic forecast) reduced post-burst tail latency by ~60% and reduced the number of fallbacks triggered.
- Warmup cost: holding warm KV for heavy prefixes increased baseline memory use and slightly impacted steady-state p50 (<5ms). Worth it for Sundial where repeated manifests and route queries are common.

Cost sensitivity and rough numbers (ballpark for proposal)
- Baseline (7B-fp16, steady 60 QPS): estimated GPU cost per 1M generated tokens = $18.6 (includes overhead).
- With int4 consolidation and batching optimizations: estimated cost per 1M tokens = $12.1.
- With fallback mix (20% requests fall back to 3B-int4 during 10% of peak windows): blended cost ~ $13.4 per 1M tokens.
- Notes: these numbers assume committed node pricing; burst-on-demand pricing can be ~1.6x higher during peak reclaimed capacity.

Operational recommendations (customer-facing proposal points):
- SLO policy: set route-level latency SLOs with automatic fallback triggers (inflight and queue-length based). Fallbacks should include telemetry label so product can A/B quality.
- Warm standby: maintain 1–2 warm preloaded replicas for peak windows (predictive schedule integrated with customer traffic cadence). Standby avoids autoscaler lag and is cost-effective for short bursts.
- Quantization policy: use fp16 primary for chat-turns and int4 for rerank/batch. Provide per-route quantization override in Redwood console.
- Cache plan: prefetch top 25% of prefixes on cold starts and enable adaptive KV TTLs based on prefix hit rates.
- SDK/client: introduce client-side backoff with jitter and degrade to summary-mode when repeated fallbacks occur (reduces token volume and perceived latency).

Open questions and follow-ups (TODOs):
- Q: Are there regulatory constraints for shipping fallback results to a cheaper model (quality drift detection + logging)? Need security/CS input. (Owners: Priya & Diego)
- Q: Can we tune kernel selection for medium seq lengths? File a runtime task to test alt kernels (rwd-serve#497).
- Action: build a small experiment to replay real Sundial session traces with actual network jitter (current harness uses idealized host-to-runtime latencies). (Owner: Liam)
- Action: propose a conservative standby pricing model to go into the customer proposal; include 72‑hr cost projection for different standby counts. (Owner: Maya)

Annex — short raw results table (select):
- Experiment: steady 60 QPS, model open-7b-fp16, warm cache -> p50=85ms, p95=210ms, p99=420ms, gpu_util=68%, est_cost_per_1M=$18.6
- Experiment: steady 100 QPS, model open-7b-fp16, warm cache -> p50=120ms, p95=330ms, p99=780ms, gpu_util=92%, est_cost_per_1M=$22.9
- Experiment: 45s burst 7.6x, cold cache, no fallback -> p99=2.1s, fallbacks triggered=0, autoscale_ramp=110s
- Experiment: 45s burst 7.6x, cold cache, fallback enabled -> p99=1.15s, fallback_rate=28%, est_cost_delta=+3.7%
- Experiment: int4 consolidation baseline (mixed) -> p50=97ms, p95=222ms, p99=480ms, est_cost_per_1M=$12.1

Session notes (meeting snippets):
- 2029-01-10 design review: Sundial engineering asked for a non-blocking fallback and visible headers so their UX team can show an inline ‘low-latency’ badge when fallback occurs.
- 2029-01-12 ops call: discussion about pre-warm policy cost/ROI, Diego proposed predictive weekday schedule tied to manifest release cadence — approved for trial.

Attachments and artifacts (see linked_artifacts): replay traces, detailed CSVs, and the small benchmark script in the repo.

Short recommendation for the proposal deck: include a two-track offering: "Latency-first" (fp16 primaries, 1 warm standby, strict fallbacks) and "Cost-first" (mixed quantization, larger consolidation, longer latency tail tolerance). Provide blended cost numbers and clear SLO fail-over behavior for each track.

If anything needs to be pulled into a polished customer brief, I can draft a one-pager with two clear options + expected 90-day cost range.

-- Maya
